Title: Binocular stereo vision-based relative positioning algorithm for drone swarm

Binocular stereo vision-based 
relative positioning algorithm for 
drone swarm
Qing Cheng1,2 & Yazhe Wang1,2
To address the challenges of high computational complexity and poor real-time performance in 
binocular vision-based Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) formation flight, this paper introduces a UAV 
localization algorithm based on a lightweight object detection model. Firstly, we optimized the 
YOLOv5s model using lightweight design principles, resulting in Yolo-SGN. This model achieves a 
65.5% reduction in parameter count, a 62.7% reduction in FLOPs, and a 1.8% increase in accuracy 
compared to the original detection model. Subsequently, Yolo-SGN is utilized to extract target regions 
from binocular images, and feature point matching is exclusively conducted within these regions to 
minimize unnecessary computations in non-target areas. Experimental results demonstrate that the 
combination of Yolo-SGN and the Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF (ORB) algorithm reduces feature 
point matching computations to only a quarter of those in the original ORB algorithm, significantly 
enhancing real-time performance. Finally, the extracted feature points from UAVs are input into a 
binocular vision localization model to compute their three-dimensional coordinates. The average of the 
three-dimensional coordinates of all feature points is used to determine the three-dimensional position 
of the target UAV. Experimental results confirm that the UAV binocular vision localization algorithm, 
based on a lightweight object detection model, exhibits exceptional performance in terms of precision 
and real-time capabilities.
Keywords  Unmanned aerial vehicle detection, Lightweight network, Binocular stereo vision, Deep learning
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are autonomous flying aircraft designed for various payloads, capable of 
performing multiple tasks and being reused. Their prominent features include exceptional cost-effectiveness, 
minimal operational losses, zero human casualties, outstanding maneuverability, potential stealthiness, and 
adaptability across various domains. These characteristics make UAVs multifunctional, adaptive, and efficient 
tools, reducing operational costs, enhancing mission safety, and increasing success rates. Consequently, UAVs 
have found widespread applications in military, civilian, and scientific research domains1–4.
Given the physical and computational limitations inherent in the mission capabilities of individual 
unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), particularly in scenarios involving extensive coverage or intricate tasks, 
the formation of UAV groups becomes a common imperative. These groups are essential for cooperative 
endeavors encompassing activities like reconnaissance, target tracking, disaster response, security patrols, and 
environmental protection5–11. When implementing UAV swarm flight, one of the key challenges is to ensure 
precise and stable relative positions among the UAVs within the swarm.
Traditional target localization techniques predominantly rely on sensors such as radar and laser. These 
sensors are susceptible to interference from other sensors onboard unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), which, in 
turn, engenders inaccuracies in the localization process. Moreover, these sensors exhibit incapacity in discerning 
specific target objects12–14. In recent years, there has been a rapid and substantial advancement in computer 
vision technology, leading to the emergence of vision-based target localization methods as a highly promising 
and burgeoning approach15,16. When compared to conventional localization techniques, vision-based methods 
present a spectrum of remarkable advantages. Firstly, vision sensors exhibit a preference for relatively permissive 
experimental environments and less stringent hardware prerequisites, thereby making them suitable for a broader 
array of scenarios17. Secondly, in contrast to certain high-cost sensors, vision sensors are distinguished by their 
lower production costs, establishing them as a cost-effective alternative18–20. Moreover, vision sensors offer the 
distinct advantage of conveying abundant information and possessing extensive detection capabilities, thereby 
presenting the potential to furnish more precise and comprehensive target localization information, particularly

Visual localization techniques are classified into two types based on the number of sensors: monocular and 
binocular localization. Monocular visual localization relies on a single visual sensor, rendering it unable to 
directly acquire depth information for objects within the field of view. This monocular approach is confined 
to furnishing two-dimensional image data, thereby introducing challenges for three-dimensional object 
localization.
In contrast, binocular visual localization capitalizes on the rotational and translational parameters between 
two visual sensors to compute disparity information, enabling the acquisition of depth information for target 
objects and, consequently, the determination of their three-dimensional positions. This ability to obtain depth 
information grants binocular visual localization a substantial advantage when it comes to tasks involving the 
three-dimensional localization of objects in space. Through the computation of disparity, binocular visual 
systems can emulate the principles of human binocular stereopsis, thereby augmenting the precision and stability 
of target position estimation. This technology is characterized by its straightforward design, high adaptability, 
and dependability, and it discovers widespread utility across diverse domains, including robot navigation, 
autonomous driving, drone navigation, medical image processing, and beyond18–20.
In response to the challenge of estimating relative positions during UAV swarm operations, this paper 
introduces a binocular stereovision-based solution, making the following primary contributions:
	(1)	 Developed a lightweight and efficient object detection model, Yolo-SGN: Yolo-SGN achieves high-pre­
cision object detection while significantly reducing computational complexity, making it well-suited for 
resource-constrained embedded system environments, especially in UAV localization tasks with high re­
al-time requirements.
	(2)	 Optimized the stereo vision localization framework: By integrating Yolo-SGN with the ORB algorithm, the 
efficiency of feature point detection and matching has been improved, significantly enhancing the real-time 
performance of the stereo vision-based 3D localization system.
	(3)	 Addressed key challenges in practical application scenarios: The study focuses on scenarios with limited 
computational resources and strict real-time requirements (e.g., UAV swarm localization), optimizing ex­
isting methods to provide an efficient and reliable solution.
This approach amalgamates critical technologies, including target detection, feature point matching, and 
binocular vision localization, providing a practical solution for the efficient operation of UAV swarms.
The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section “Related work” offers an extensive review of 
relevant research on target detection. Section “Methods” elaborates on the proposed method, and Section 
“Results” encompasses the results of its application. Lastly, Section “Discussion” provides the concluding remarks.
Related work
Object detection algorithm grounded in Convolutional Neural Network
Visual object detection involves identifying, recognizing, and labeling particular objects in images, which is 
closely associated with object classification, tracking, and image segmentation. Conventional object detection 
approaches22–24 generally utilize a sliding window technique to scan the entire image for potential object 
locations. Subsequently, hand-crafted features, including scale-invariant feature transform25 and histogram 
of oriented gradients26, are extracted from the image window, followed by classification using support vector 
machine (SVM) or AdaBoost classifiers. However, traditional object detection algorithms based on the sliding 
window strategy have issues of high computational complexity, limited efficiency in detecting objects, and 
difficulty in handling changes in object shape and background. Additionally, designing hand-crafted features for 
each new object class requires considerable time.
Recently, due to the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence technology and the advancement of object 
detection techniques founded on deep learning and computer vision, object detection algorithms utilizing 
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have exhibited remarkable performance in detection and recognition 
when compared to conventional machine learning approaches. This progress has led to the emergence of 
numerous CNN-based detection methods. At present, computer vision-based object detection algorithms can be 
broadly categorized into two groups. The first category comprises two-stage object detection models, with Faster 
R-CNN as a prominent example27. In contrast, the second category encompasses one-stage object detection 
models, with notable representatives such as YOLO28,29 and SSD30.Two-stage object detection models enhance 
detection accuracy by training region proposal networks to produce object candidate boxes. Nevertheless, their 
structural and parameter redundancy poses challenges in achieving rapid detection. In contrast, one-stage object 
detection models offer a key advantage: they eliminate the need for a region proposal network. After training 
the backbone feature extraction network, they directly conduct classification and regression on the input data. 
This significantly reduces training and inference times, establishing one-stage object detection models as the 
prevailing choice in current practice31–33.
Lightweight object detection algorithm
In the context of vision target tracking, the real-time performance of the object detection algorithm plays a 
pivotal role. However, the computation required by mainstream target detection algorithms is currently too 
high, and the processing speed of these algorithms on images collected by computers is too slow, resulting in a 
lack of real-time tracking capability for UAVs. Therefore, the use of a fast object detection algorithm is essential 
for machine vision target tracking in UAVs34.

Lightweight object detection is a methodology aimed at enhancing the operational efficiency of object 
detection models in resource-constrained environments, such as embedded devices and mobile platforms, 
by reducing the model’s size and computational complexity. This theory focuses on minimizing the volume 
and computational overhead of object detection models while maintaining a satisfactory level of detection 
performance35–37.
The theoretical foundations of lightweight object detection primarily encompass the following aspects:
•	 Model structure simplification: This involves reducing the complexity of the neural network structure by 
designing simpler architectures. This includes decreasing the number of layers, channels, parameters, etc., to 
lower the overall complexity of the model.
•	 Parameter compression: Techniques such as parameter pruning and quantization are employed to decrease 
the model’s parameter size, thereby reducing storage requirements and computational burdens.
•	 Design of lightweight models: Models are specifically tailored for object detection tasks with an emphasis on 
lightweight design to maintain high detection performance on embedded devices.
•	 Knowledge distillation: This approach enhances the performance of smaller, simplified models by transfer­
ring knowledge from larger, more complex models, simultaneously reducing the overall model size.
•	 Hardware acceleration: Dedicated hardware, such as GPUs or TPUs, or customized hardware architectures, is 
leveraged to boost the inference speed of object detection models.
In summary, the theory of lightweight object detection aims to achieve the efficient deployment of object 
detection models in resource-constrained environments, making it suitable for scenarios like embedded systems 
and mobile devices.
Visual localization methods
Visual localization methods can be broadly classified based on different technical principles and application 
scenarios. The primary categories are as follows:
	(1)	 Geometry-based methods: This category primarily relies on geometric principles, such as triangulation, 
to estimate the three-dimensional position of objects. By utilizing the relative positions between multiple 
cameras or sensors, depth information of the object is calculated. These methods perform well in well-lit 
environments with sufficient viewpoints and offer high computational efficiency, making them commonly 
used in scene reconstruction and stereoscopic localization13–38.
	(2)	 Feature point matching-based methods: These methods detect feature points in images and match them 
across images captured from different perspectives to estimate the object’s position. Typically, they combine 
feature extraction and description algorithms, enabling relatively precise localization39.
	(3)	 Image retrieval-based methods: This category treats the visual localization problem as an image retrieval 
task. It leverages a pre-constructed visual map and determines the location of an object or scene by match­
ing image similarities. It is primarily applied in large-scale indoor and outdoor localization tasks and is 
well-suited for handling precise geographic location matching, such as urban localization for autonomous 
vehicles40–42.
	(4)	 Sensor fusion-based methods: These methods integrate information from various sensors, such as camer­
as, LiDAR, and inertial measurement units (IMUs), to achieve high-precision localization through sensor 
data fusion techniques. They are robust in situations where lighting conditions are poor or when image 
information is incomplete, making them suitable for real-time scenarios like autonomous driving or drone 
navigation43.
Binocular stereo vision measuring method
Stereoscopic depth estimation is a technique that replicates the human visual principle of binocular vision to 
acquire depth information about a scene. In this approach, two cameras (or sensors) are positioned at a certain 
distance, emulating the binocular observation of the same scene by human eyes. By analyzing the disparities 
between corresponding points in images captured by the two cameras, the distance from the target object to the 
cameras can be calculated13–38,44,45.
The fundamental principles of stereoscopic depth estimation involve the following steps:
•	 Camera Calibration: Prior to initiating the depth estimation process, calibration of the stereo cameras is 
necessary to determine the intrinsic parameters (internal parameters of the cameras, such as focal length and 
principal point) and extrinsic parameters (external parameters, such as the relative position and orientation 
between the cameras).
•	 Image Acquisition: Capture images of the same scene using the stereo cameras. These two images should 
exhibit a certain disparity in the horizontal direction, indicating a horizontal displacement between corre­
sponding points of the same object in the two images.
•	 Feature Matching: Identify corresponding feature points in the two images, utilizing feature matching algo­
rithms such as SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) or ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF).
•	 Disparity Calculation: Determine the horizontal displacement, or disparity, of corresponding feature points 
to understand the positional differences of objects in the images. Disparity is inversely proportional to the 
distance from the object to the cameras; thus, a larger disparity indicates a closer distance.
•	 Depth Calculation: Utilize the disparity and camera parameters to apply the principles of triangulation, cal­
culating the depth information of the object from the cameras. This process is typically implemented through 
a Disparity Map, where each pixel corresponds to the disparity value of the corresponding point in the scene.

Methods
In the process of drone target localization, we initially introduced a lightweight drone target detection model, 
referred to as Yolo-SGN. The principal aim of this model is to efficiently identify and extract drone target 
regions from the acquired raw binocular images. Next, we applied the ORB algorithm to extract and match 
feature points in the target regions of binocular images. This approach significantly reduces the algorithm’s 
computational burden by excluding unnecessary computations in non-target regions, thereby enhancing its real-
time performance. Finally, we applied the principles of binocular stereovision to integrate information from the 
binocular images and conduct stereo disparity analysis. This process enabled us to deduce three-dimensional 
coordinates based on the pixel coordinates of feature points. By averaging the three-dimensional coordinates of 
all feature points, we achieved precise drone target localization.
Object recognition algorithm for drones based on lightweight YOLOv5s (Yolo-SGN)
The original YOLOv5s network
YOLOv5s is a highly efficient object detection model and the smallest in scale in the YOLOv5 series46. The model 
uses a lightweight backbone network and a multi-scale feature fusion and efficient output prediction strategy to 
achieve efficient, accurate, and real-time object detection47,48.
The YOLOv5s network model structure comprises four main components: an input end, a backbone 
network, a feature fusion module, and an output end. The input end employs the Mosaic-4 data augmentation 
technique, which enhances image information by employing cropping, splicing, and scaling operations, making 
it particularly suitable for small object detection. The backbone network utilizes CSPDarknet53 as the feature 
extractor, enhancing feature extraction capabilities while maintaining efficiency. The feature fusion module 
combines the Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) and Pyramid Attention Network (PAN) structures to strengthen 
the features extracted by the backbone network, thus improving the network’s feature fusion capabilities. The 
output end incorporates an efficient prediction strategy, encompassing the use of multi-scale feature maps within 
the backbone network, feature fusion within convolution layers, and streamlined processing in the output layer 
to achieve both rapid and accurate object detection.
In comparison to other models within the YOLOv5 series, YOLOv5s stands out for its smaller model size 
and quicker inference speed, albeit with a slightly lower accuracy when contrasted with larger models. The 
model exhibits commendable performance on various public object detection datasets and has found extensive 
application in practical scenarios, including but not limited to intelligent surveillance, autonomous driving, and 
robotic vision.The original YOLOv5s structure is illustrated in Fig. 1.

size. Secondly, the C3 module in the feature fusion section is substituted with a C3Ghost module comprised

Lightweight feature extraction
We have implemented two significant modifications to the feature extraction network. Firstly, we replaced C3 
with SF, and secondly, we altered the downsampling segment of the main network after C3 to GS.
The SF network structure is visually depicted in Fig. 3. Within the SF network, the Input undergoes channel 
separation through a combination of 1 × 1 convolution and channel split operations, resulting in the creation of 
two sub-features, namely the blue and yellow features. Sub-feature 1 (yellow) remains unaltered, while sub-feature 
2 (blue) proceeds to the S module for feature learning. After the learning process within the S module, the blue 
feature undergoes another pass through the S module, ultimately yielding the green feature. The incorporation 
of yellow, blue, and green multi-scale features, followed by their concatenation, strengthens feature reuse and 
is further processed through a 1 × 1 convolution layer to yield the output feature. This method, inspired by 
VOVNet49, leverages multi-scale feature concatenation and feature reuse.
The S module is comprised of two 3 × 3 grouped convolution layers, incorporating channel shuffle operations 
to facilitate interaction among features from different groups. This design concept is inspired by ShuffleNet50 
and is aimed at achieving more efficient feature communication and utilization. These modifications and 
structural enhancements aim to further optimize the feature extraction network, thereby improving its detection 
performance for intricate targets.
The inspiration behind the GS network structure design originates from the downsampling strategy utilized 
in PeleeNet51, as visually depicted in Fig. 3. The Stemblock structure present in PeleeNet notably amplifies the 
network’s capacity for expressing features, all while concurrently diminishing the model’s parameter count. 
Within the GS network structure, we have incorporated a clever branching scheme: one branch combines max-
pooling and 1 × 1 convolution to halve the channel count, while the other branch employs a 3x3 convolution 
with a stride of 2 to achieve an equivalent reduction in channel count. Subsequently, the outputs of these two 
branches are concatenated to produce the final output feature. This design assures that the network efficiently 
reduces its parameter count without overly compromising vital semantic information. The judicious application 
of this feature fusion strategy contributes significantly to enhancing the model’s performance, thereby yielding 
outstanding results in visual detection tasks.

ORB algorithm
The ORB algorithm comprises three main components: feature point extraction, feature point description, and 
feature point matching. It is a combination and enhancement of the FAST (Features from Accelerated Segment 
Test) extraction algorithm and the BRIEF (Binary Robust Independent Elementary Features) description 
algorithm. While both the FAST and BRIEF algorithms demonstrate high computational efficiency, they do not 
possess rotational and scale invariance. In the ORB algorithm, rotational invariance is achieved by defining the 
orientation angle of feature points based on these two algorithms.
The FAST algorithm is primarily designed to detect areas with prominent local pixel intensity changes and 
is renowned for its high speed. The core concept of this algorithm is based on the observation that if a pixel 
exhibits a substantial difference in intensity (either brighter or darker) compared to its neighboring pixels, it is 
more likely to be a corner. In contrast to other corner detection algorithms, FAST achieves its efficiency by solely 
comparing pixel intensities. The specific steps involved in the algorithm are visually depicted in Fig. 6.

BRIEF is a binary descriptor comprising a vector of 0s and 1s. This descriptor encodes the relationship between 
two neighboring pixels (e.g., p and q) near the keypoint, where a value of 1 indicates that pixel p is greater than 
pixel q, and a value of 0 indicates the opposite. By selecting 128 pairs of such pixels (p and q), a 128-dimensional 
vector consisting of binary values is generated. The fundamental concept behind the BRIEF algorithm involves 
selecting N pairs of points surrounding the keypoint P in a specific pattern and combining the outcomes of these 
N pairwise comparisons to construct the descriptor.
Following feature extraction and description through the ORB algorithm, the similarity between two feature 
points is established by considering the distance between their respective descriptor vectors. To locate matching 
points, the distances between the feature points in the left eye image and all the feature points in the right eye 
image are calculated, and the pair with the shortest distance is designated as a match. As the BRIEF feature 
descriptor algorithm leverages binary strings to represent features, the Hamming distance is utilized as a measure 
of similarity between two feature points.

(1) YOLOv5-SGN Object Detection
YOLOv5-SGN achieves faster inference speed by reducing model parameters and computational complexity 
while maintaining accuracy, making it particularly suitable for object detection tasks in UAV-related scenarios. 
The key roles of YOLOv5-SGN in this method include:
•	 Real-time Performance: YOLOv5-SGN exhibits excellent real-time performance, quickly detecting objects in 
the images captured by stereo cameras, ensuring that object detection does not become a bottleneck in the 
system.
•	 Lightweight Design: The lightweight design of the YOLOv5 network optimizes computational costs, making 
it ideal for embedded devices or scenarios with limited computational power.
•	 Robustness: The efficient convolution operations in YOLOv5-SGN allow it to stably detect objects in complex 
scenes (such as under varying lighting conditions), providing reliable initial inputs for subsequent stereo 
matching.
(2) ORB feature matching
ORB offers robust feature matching performance while maintaining low computational complexity, 
making it well-suited for embedded systems and real-time applications. In this method, ORB is used to locate 
corresponding feature points of the target object in stereo images, enabling accurate 3D reconstruction and 
localization. The primary steps of ORB in stereo localization include:
•	 Keypoint Detection: The ORB algorithm extracts keypoints within the target region from both the left and 
right camera images. ORB uses an improved FAST algorithm for corner detection and combines it with Har­
ris corner responses to select high-quality keypoints.
•	 Feature Description and Matching: ORB calculates feature descriptors at the detected keypoints using the 
BRIEF algorithm and matches keypoints between the left and right images by comparing the Hamming dis­
tance, thereby identifying corresponding object features in both images.
•	 Eliminating Mismatches: To improve matching accuracy, the RANSAC algorithm is applied to eliminate mis­
matched points, ensuring the reliability of matched pairs.(3) Stereo localization
After YOLOv5-SGN detects the target region and ORB identifies corresponding keypoints in the left and right 
images, the depth information of the object can be calculated based on the geometric principles of stereo vision. 
The specific steps are as follows:
•	 Disparity Calculation: Disparity refers to the horizontal shift between corresponding points of the same ob­
ject in the left and right images. The disparity is computed based on the matched feature points’ positions in 
the two images.

Experimental environment
The training environment for all models in this experiment was Windows 10, with an AMD Ryzen 5 4600H with 
Radeon Graphics 3.00 GHz CPU, 16 GB of RAM, an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1660 Ti GPU, and Pytorch as the 
deep learning framework. The Python version used was 3.7.
During the calibration process, we first performed intrinsic parameter calibration for both the left and right 
cameras to obtain the intrinsic matrices for each camera (including focal length and principal point coordinates) 
as well as the distortion parameters of the lenses. Subsequently, through stereo calibration, we computed the 
extrinsic parameters of the two cameras, namely the rotation matrix and translation vector, thereby determining 
the spatial geometric relationship between the two cameras. These parameters are critical inputs for the 
calibration process and are described by the parameters listed in Table 1.
Next, we applied a stereo rectification algorithm to process the images from the left and right cameras. 
Specifically, we performed image transformations based on epipolar geometry, aligning the image planes of 
the two cameras to be coplanar and ensuring that the corresponding epipolar lines are horizontally aligned. To 
achieve this, we used the stereoRectify function from the OpenCV library, which calculates the rectification 
matrices using the input intrinsic and extrinsic parameter matrices. By applying the rectification matrices (using 
the initUndistortRectifyMap and remap functions), the left and right images were remapped onto the rectified 
image planes.
After completing the rectification, the epipolar lines of all corresponding point pairs became parallel, 
ensuring that feature points could be searched only along the horizontal direction during image matching and 
triangulation calculations. This significantly improved the efficiency and accuracy of the algorithm.

Ablation experiments of feature fusion network models
In the conducted ablation experiments, YOLOv5s was employed as the baseline model. Model A was derived 
by substituting the backbone network of YOLOv5s with SF-GS. Building upon this modification, Model B was 
obtained by replacing the original C3 module in the feature fusion section with the C3Ghost module. Model C 
was created by substituting the Conv module in the original feature fusion section PANet with NextConv.
The outcomes of the ablation experiments are summarized in Table 3. The data unmistakably demonstrate 
that when the backbone network of YOLOv5s was replaced with SF-GS, both C3Ghost and NextConv models 
led to a reduction in parameter count and an improvement in accuracy for Model A. Specifically, Model B 
exhibited a 32% decrease in parameter count and a 39% reduction in FLOPs compared to Model A, accompanied 
by a 0.6% increase in mAP0.5. Similarly, Model C demonstrated a 25% reduction in parameter count and a 4% 
decrease in FLOPs compared to Model A, along with a 0.4% increase in mAP0.5. Consequently, our hypothesis 
was that NextConv could enhance model accuracy while simultaneously reducing parameter count and FLOPs. 
To investigate this further, we introduced NextConv based on Model B, resulting in the creation of Model D. 
Table 3 reveals that Model D experienced a 36.6% reduction in parameter count, a 3.3% decrease in FLOPs, and a 
0.3% increase in mAP0.5 compared to Model B. Finally, Model E (Yolo-SGN) was obtained by applying the EIoU 
loss function to Model D, further enhancing the accuracy of object detection. This experiment serves to validate 
the improved model’s performance, with Yolo-SGN effectively striking a balance between speed and accuracy 
through a reduction in parameter count, ultimately surpassing the detection accuracy of the original YOLOv5s.

Experimental results of target localization
In the static validation experiment, the target UAV was made to hover at the same altitude as the stereo cameras 
mounted on the test UAV, positioned 5 meters away from the test UAV, for multiple localization measurements 
to validate our algorithm. Fig. 14 presents the experimental results of stereo distance measurement, with the 
vertical axis representing the relative distance of the UAV and the horizontal axis representing the sequence 
of experiments. A total of 300 measurements were conducted with the UAV in a hovering state to verify the 
accuracy of the stereo distance estimation provided by the algorithm.
During the experiment, it was necessary to ensure that the UAV maintained a stable hover, so that the test 
data could be reliably used to evaluate the stability and accuracy of the algorithm. Results show that under 
static conditions (UAV hovering without horizontal displacement), the maximum distance error was 3.21%, 
and the average error was only 1.52%. These results demonstrate the excellent performance of our algorithm in 
accurately localizing static UAV targets.
In the localization experiment, the target UAV flew at the same altitude as the stereo cameras mounted on 
the observing UAV (both at a height of 2 m). The target UAV flew from the left side to the right side of the stereo 
cameras at a speed of 10 m per second, with the minimum horizontal distance between the target UAV and the 
observing UAV being 10 m. This experiment aimed to simulate the lateral movement of the target UAV and 
evaluate the performance of the proposed relative localization model in dynamic scenarios. In the localization 
experiment, we assumed that the UAV remained in good operational condition, maintained a constant speed 
of 10 m/s, and flew at a constant altitude of 2 m, neglecting the influence of wind speed, thus assuming that the 
UAV’s trajectory was a straight line parallel to the ground. The observed UAV coordinates were compared with 
the theoretical UAV coordinates along the X, Y, and Z axes to calculate errors.
The proposed localization algorithm achieved average errors of 3.8%, 2.1%, and 1.7% in the X, Y, and Z 
directions, respectively. Figure 15 specifically shows the spatial arrangement of the observed position points, 
demonstrating that the observed UAV flight trajectory closely matches the actual flight path. This indicates that 
the proposed algorithm can effectively measure the relative position of the target UAV in an air-to-air scenario.
Discussion
To address the issues of poor real-time performance and high computational complexity in binocular 
vision-based UAV localization, this study proposes a UAV binocular vision localization algorithm based on 
a lightweight object detection model. In the field of UAV target recognition, we have optimized the original 
YOLOv5s model by adopting lightweight design principles, thus achieving high-precision and fast UAV target 
detection. For binocular vision-based localization, we utilize a lightweight detection model to extract target 
regions. By performing feature point recognition exclusively within these target regions, we significantly 
reduce the computational complexity associated with the ORB algorithm. Furthermore, the reduction in the
